justice: The street provides space for multiple modes, with travel lanes, curbside parking, sidewalks, and shopfront access visible on the right side.
Resource distribution appears imbalanced because most of the carriageway is dedicated to motor vehicles, while no dedicated protected bicycle lane is visible.
Accessibility is only moderate: the right-side sidewalk exists, but it is narrowed by parked vehicles, scooters near storefronts, tree pits, and utility/light poles.
Fairness is reduced because cyclists and pedestrians appear to share edge space indirectly while cars receive clearer lane allocation and smoother movement space.
safety: Moving cars, scooters, and motorcycles are using the same roadway without visible protected separation, increasing conflict risk among road users.
Several vehicles are parked directly along the curb in front of shops, which can create dooring risk and obscure pedestrians stepping into the street.
The road markings are visible and the pavement surface looks smooth, which supports basic traffic legibility for drivers.
Large street trees on the right improve enclosure and visual comfort, but they also cast partial shadows that may hide curbside activity around parked vehicles and scooters.
livability: Active ground-floor shops on the right provide daily services and contribute to a functional neighborhood street environment.
The row of storefronts, awnings, and visible parked scooters suggests regular local commerce and street-level activity.
Street trees add greenery and make the corridor feel more inhabited and less barren than a fully hardscaped road.
Livability is weakened by the dominance of moving traffic and curbside parking, which leaves limited visible public space for staying, socializing, or recreation.
sustainability: The mature street trees provide ecosystem benefits such as shade and some cooling, supporting environmental performance at the street level.
Mixed-use frontage with neighborhood shops can reduce travel distances for everyday needs and support local service access.
No dedicated cycling infrastructure is visible, limiting support for low-carbon transport choices beyond walking and scooters.
The street appears heavily oriented toward private vehicle movement and curbside parking, which weakens overall transport sustainability.
aesthetics: The large street trees create a strong green canopy on the right and improve the visual quality of the corridor.
Continuous shop awnings and a consistent street wall give the right side of the street a recognizable urban character.
The left side is visually weakened by a long construction wall and a stark unfinished building, reducing overall scenic coherence.
Clean asphalt and orderly lane markings help the street appear maintained, though the visual environment remains dominated by traffic and parked vehicles.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: the large trees on the right provide meaningful shade, but the broad exposed asphalt roadway receives intense direct sunlight.
Physical comfort for pedestrians appears limited because the sidewalk edge is interrupted by poles, tree pits, scooters, and curbside parking activity.
Psychological comfort is reduced by the close presence of moving traffic, motorcycles in the lane, and vehicles parked tightly beside the walking area.
Shop awnings offer some localized shade and weather protection along the right frontage, improving comfort for people near storefronts.
walkability: A sidewalk is present on the right side and the active storefronts provide destinations within walking distance.
Walkability is constrained because the pedestrian zone appears narrow and cluttered by poles, trees, scooters, and parked vehicles near the curb.
No marked crosswalk or pedestrian-priority treatment is visible in this scene, reducing crossing convenience and route continuity.
Traffic volume and speed environment appear moderate to high relative to the available pedestrian space, making walking feel less protected.
bikeability: No dedicated bike lane or protected cycling track is visible anywhere in the roadway.
Cyclists would need to mix with cars, vans, and motorcycles in general traffic, which reduces perceived and actual cycling safety.
Curbside parked vehicles create potential dooring conflicts for anyone riding near the edge of the road.
The smooth pavement and relatively straight corridor support rideability, but the lack of separation and bike-specific markings keeps bikeability low.
